nameStory: Snake's-head fritillary gets its name from its drooping, bell-shaped flower that resembles a snake's head when viewed from the side. The word 'fritillary' comes from the Latin 'fritillus,' meaning dice box, referring to the checkered pattern on the petals that looks like a checkerboard or chess piece.
description: Snake's-head fritillary is a small, elegant spring bulb that produces a single nodding flower on a slender stem. The distinctive bell-shaped bloom hangs downward like a drooping tulip, displaying a remarkable checkerboard pattern in purple and white. Growing 8-12 inches tall, this European native has narrow, grass-like leaves that emerge from an underground bulb. Though rare in New England, it occasionally appears in naturalized garden settings or escaped populations.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single drooping bell-shaped flower with a distinctive checkerboard pattern of purple and white squares, hanging downward on a slender stem like a nodding lantern

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that are blue-green in color and feel smooth to the touch, growing alternately up the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single upright stem 8-12 inches tall emerging from underground bulb, with the characteristic drooping flower at the top

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Three-chambered capsule that splits open to release flat, papery seeds after the flower fades

habitat: In New England, snake's-head fritillary is extremely rare, appearing occasionally in moist meadows, naturalized garden areas, or escaped from cultivation. It prefers rich, well-drained soil that stays moist in spring but can dry somewhat in summer. Look for it in areas with partial shade to full sun, often near old homesteads or abandoned gardens.

seasonality.spring: Blooms in April to early May with its distinctive checkered flowers appearing before many other plants leaf out fully. Leaves emerge early in spring as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Foliage begins to die back after flowering as the plant enters dormancy. Seed capsules ripen and split open to release seeds.
seasonality.fall: Plant is completely dormant with no above-ground growth visible. Bulb rests underground until the following spring.
seasonality.winter: No visible growth above ground as the bulb remains dormant in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to trigger new growth.

funFact: This flower was once called 'leper lily' because its drooping, bell-shaped bloom resembled the warning bells that people with leprosy were required to carry in medieval times to announce their presence.
confusionNotes: The drooping, checkered flower is so distinctive that it's rarely confused with other plants. Young shoots might be mistaken for grass or small bulb foliage, but once the unique checkerboard flower appears, identification becomes unmistakable.
contextualKnowledge: Snake's-head fritillary has many colorful common names including guinea-hen flower, chess flower, and Lazarus bell, reflecting people's fascination with its unusual checkered pattern. Despite being in the lily family, it looks quite different from typical lilies with its single drooping flower and unique coloration.
compareHints: As the only fritillary species recorded in New England, snake's-head fritillary is unique in the region. Within the lily family, it differs dramatically from other members like trout lilies or wild leeks by its distinctive checkered pattern and single drooping flower. Unlike upward-facing lilies, this species always nods downward, and no other lily family plant in New England displays the characteristic checkerboard pattern.
